en.statement: Changes made inside a container update the image it started from.
en.explanation: A container writes changes to its own writable filesystem. Its source image remains read-only.

en.statement: On Linux, a container runs its own kernel like a virtual machine.
en.explanation: Linux containers on one host share its kernel. A virtual machine runs a separate operating system with its own kernel.

en.statement: Docker uses Linux namespaces to isolate a container's process view.
en.explanation: Namespaces limit which host and other-container processes a container normally sees.

en.statement: Docker uses cgroups to enforce a configured CPU quota for a container.
en.explanation: When a CPU quota is configured, Docker changes the container's cgroup settings on the Linux host.

en.statement: The docker CLI executes container processes after contacting dockerd.
en.explanation: The docker CLI sends commands to dockerd. The daemon carries out container operations.

en.statement: The Docker Engine API accepts client requests over a Unix socket.
en.explanation: A Unix socket is one transport for REST API communication with the Docker daemon.

en.statement: With the active docker context pointing at a remote host's daemon, `docker ps` lists the local machine's containers.
en.explanation: The CLI sends each command to the daemon chosen by -H, DOCKER_HOST or the active docker context, which can be a remote host reached over SSH or TCP. With none of these set, it uses the local daemon socket.

en.statement: On macOS, Docker Desktop runs Linux containers on the macOS kernel.
en.explanation: Docker Desktop runs its daemon and Linux containers inside a lightweight Linux VM on macOS.

source.title: Understand permission requirements for Docker Desktop on Mac

en.statement: Docker Desktop bundles dockerd and the docker CLI in its installation.
en.explanation: Docker Desktop packages the daemon and client together for local container development.

en.statement: docker commit creates a new image from a container's file changes.
en.explanation: docker commit captures filesystem changes from a container as a reusable image.

en.statement: docker run -d detaches the CLI while the container's main process runs.
en.explanation: The -d flag starts the container in the background instead of occupying the terminal.

en.statement: docker run --entrypoint sh app passes sh as an argument to the image's executable.
en.explanation: The --entrypoint flag replaces the image's default executable for that container; sh becomes the executable.

en.statement: docker create prepares a container that docker start can launch later.
en.explanation: docker create sets up a container from an image and leaves it in the created state until it is started.

en.statement: docker stop waits after sending the configured stop signal before forcing termination.
en.explanation: docker stop first sends the container's stop signal and uses SIGKILL if the process remains after the grace period.

en.statement: An on-failure restart policy restarts a container after a successful exit.
en.explanation: The on-failure policy restarts a container after a non-zero exit code. A successful exit does not trigger it.

en.statement: docker rm --force sends SIGKILL to remove a running container.
en.explanation: The --force option kills a running container's main process before removing the container.

en.statement: docker exec can start a stopped container to run the requested command.
en.explanation: docker exec runs a new command inside a running container. Start a stopped container first.

en.statement: docker run exits with code 127 when a container command lacks execute permission.
en.explanation: Exit code 127 means Docker cannot find the container command. Code 126 means it found the command but could not invoke it.

en.statement: Docker assigns a hard memory limit to a new container with unconfigured resources.
en.explanation: A container has no Docker resource limit by default. Set a runtime memory option to impose one.

en.statement: An ARG declared before the first FROM can choose the base image in FROM.
en.explanation: A global ARG declared before FROM supplies a build-time value that FROM can use in its image reference.

en.statement: RUN executes its command when a container starts from the built image.
en.explanation: RUN executes during the image build and records its filesystem result for later build steps.

en.statement: COPY extracts a local tar archive into the destination directory during the build.
en.explanation: ADD extracts a supported local tar archive by default. COPY transfers the archive as a file.

en.statement: Shell-form ENTRYPOINT drops CMD's default arguments when the container starts.
en.explanation: Docker runs a shell-form ENTRYPOINT through a command shell, so CMD defaults are not passed to the intended executable.

en.statement: A container started from the image sees the Dockerfile's ARG values as environment variables.
en.explanation: ARG supplies build-time values. ENV sets environment values that persist in the built image.

en.statement: EXPOSE publishes the declared port on the host when a container starts.
en.explanation: EXPOSE documents an intended container port. Publishing it to the host requires a runtime port mapping.

en.statement: HEALTHCHECK can flag a stalled service while its main process still runs.
en.explanation: A HEALTHCHECK runs a probe inside the container and can detect a service that remains running but stops responding.

en.statement: STOPSIGNAL changes the signal sent by Ctrl+C to the container process.
en.explanation: STOPSIGNAL configures Docker's stop signal. Ctrl+C sends SIGINT independently of that image instruction.

en.statement: The # syntax parser directive selects the Dockerfile frontend for a build.
en.explanation: The # syntax directive declares which Dockerfile syntax version BuildKit uses to interpret the file.

en.statement: `COPY <<EOF /app.sh` runs the heredoc lines in the default shell during the build.
en.explanation: A COPY heredoc writes the here-document content to the destination file, here /app.sh. A RUN heredoc with no command is the form the default shell executes.

en.statement: docker build bypasses Buildx and sends its requests straight to BuildKit.
en.explanation: docker build wraps Buildx; Buildx interprets the options and sends the build request to BuildKit.

en.statement: COPY can read a host file beside the Dockerfile even when it lies outside the build context.
en.explanation: COPY reads local sources from the selected build context. The Dockerfile's own location does not extend that context.

en.statement: A Git URL supplies its repository and submodules as the build context.
en.explanation: For a Git build context, the builder clones the repository and its submodules for build instructions to access.

en.statement: For remote tarballs, the docker CLI downloads the context before BuildKit starts.
en.explanation: The CLI sends a remote tarball URL to the builder. BuildKit downloads the archive on the host where its daemon runs.

en.statement: A Dockerfile piped as the entire build input gives COPY an empty local filesystem context.
en.explanation: When plain Dockerfile text is the entire build input, the build has no local files for COPY to read.

en.statement: .dockerignore filters files after the builder receives the build context.
en.explanation: The build client applies .dockerignore patterns before sending matching context files to the builder.

en.statement: A Dockerfile-specific ignore file takes precedence over the context's .dockerignore.
en.explanation: When both files exist, Docker uses the ignore file associated with the selected Dockerfile in preference to the context-root .dockerignore.

en.statement: --build-context replaces the default positional build context with a named source.
en.explanation: --build-context adds a named source alongside the positional default context; it does not replace that context.

en.statement: In Docker Engine 29, Docker selects the legacy builder for ordinary Linux image builds.
en.explanation: BuildKit is the default builder for Linux images in Docker Engine 29. The legacy Linux builder is deprecated.

en.statement: docker build --check reports Dockerfile issues while skipping build execution.
en.explanation: The --check flag runs build checks against the Dockerfile and options instead of executing the build steps.

en.statement: A stage named with `FROM alpine AS build` serves as the base of a later `FROM build` stage.
en.explanation: A later `FROM build` starts from the filesystem produced by the earlier stage named `build`.

en.statement: `COPY --from=build app /app` reads app relative to the build stage's WORKDIR.
en.explanation: `COPY --from` resolves its source path from the source stage's filesystem root, regardless of that stage's WORKDIR.

en.statement: `COPY --from=0` copies from the stage that the first FROM instruction in the Dockerfile starts.
en.explanation: Unnamed stages are referenced by integer, starting at 0 for the first FROM. Naming stages with AS keeps COPY --from working if the stages are reordered later.

en.statement: A build with `COPY --from=nginx:latest` stops with an error when nginx:latest is missing locally.
en.explanation: When --from names an image instead of a stage, Docker pulls that image if necessary during the build and copies the file from it.

en.statement: `docker build --target test` makes the test stage the image build result.
en.explanation: `--target test` selects the named test stage as the build result, which is useful for building a test or debug stage.

en.statement: BuildKit builds unrelated earlier stages while producing a selected `--target`.
en.explanation: BuildKit builds the selected target and its dependencies; it skips earlier stages that the target does not need.

en.statement: When Docker pulls a multi-platform image, its manifest list guides platform variant selection.
en.explanation: A manifest list points to platform-specific manifests. Docker selects a matching variant when it pulls the image.

en.statement: `FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM` runs a stage on the builder's native platform.
en.explanation: `BUILDPLATFORM` identifies the build node's platform; using it in `FROM` keeps that stage on the native platform.

en.statement: BuildKit exposes TARGETPLATFORM to RUN instructions before a stage declares ARG TARGETPLATFORM.
en.explanation: BuildKit defines automatic platform arguments globally. A stage needs `ARG TARGETPLATFORM` before its `RUN` instructions receive that value.

en.statement: An image layer stores the complete filesystem produced up to its Dockerfile step.
en.explanation: An image layer records filesystem changes, such as additions, modifications, and deletions, rather than a full filesystem snapshot.

en.statement: Images built from the same base image reuse its layers when stored on one Docker host.
en.explanation: Shared base layers can be stored once and reused across images, reducing storage and download work.

en.statement: With unchanged build inputs, a cached `RUN apt-get update` reruns when the remote index changes.
en.explanation: BuildKit does not refresh a cached RUN step merely because a remote package index changed. An unchanged command and build inputs can produce a cache hit.

en.statement: Changing just a source file's mtime leaves the COPY and ADD cache checksum unchanged.
en.explanation: BuildKit checks source file metadata for COPY and ADD cache matches, but excludes modification time from the checksum.

en.statement: After one RUN step misses the cache, BuildKit reuses cache for later RUN steps in that stage with unchanged text.
en.explanation: Once a step misses the cache, later RUN steps in that stage rebuild even with unchanged text, because each runs on the previous step's result.

en.statement: Changing a declared ARG value can invalidate a later RUN step that never expands the variable.
en.explanation: A declared ARG enters the RUN environment implicitly, so changing its value can cause a cache miss even when the command text stays the same.

en.statement: Changing a build secret's value invalidates the cached RUN step that consumes it.
en.explanation: BuildKit excludes secret contents from the build cache key. Changing a secret value alone does not invalidate the cached RUN step.

en.statement: With its default mode, `--cache-to` exports cache only for layers that end up in the final image.
en.explanation: The default mode=min caches only layers exported into the resulting image; mode=max also caches the layers of intermediate steps, for more cache hits.

en.statement: `docker build --no-cache` also fetches a fresh base image from the registry.
en.explanation: `--no-cache` reruns build steps. `--pull` checks for a newer base image; the two flags serve separate purposes.

en.statement: In `registry.example.com/team/api:v2`, `team/api` identifies a repository inside the registry.
en.explanation: `registry.example.com` is the registry host, while `team` is the namespace and `api` is the repository.

en.statement: The image reference `alpine` resolves under Docker Hub's `library` namespace.
en.explanation: Docker uses the `library` namespace for a Docker Hub image reference that omits its namespace.

en.statement: When a tag is omitted, Docker selects the repository's most recently pushed tag.
en.explanation: Docker uses the tag literally named `latest` when an image reference omits its tag. That name does not guarantee the newest image.

en.statement: A Docker image can carry several tags that refer to the same local image ID.
en.explanation: Several tags may name the same local image ID; adding a tag does not duplicate that image's layers.

en.statement: A Dockerfile base pinned by an image digest follows updates published under its former tag.
en.explanation: A digest-pinned `FROM` keeps using the same base image version when a publisher moves a tag. Updating the base requires changing the digest.

en.statement: When `docker login` saves credentials directly to `config.json`, it encrypts them first.
en.explanation: Without a credential store, Docker writes credentials to config.json only base64-encoded, which anyone can reverse. A credential store keeps them in an external store such as the OS keychain or pass.

en.statement: `docker image push` takes its destination registry from the host part of the image reference.
en.explanation: To publish to a self-hosted registry, you first tag the image as host:port/name, and Docker pushes to the registry named in that reference.

en.statement: Docker Hub's Verified Publisher badge identifies Docker-maintained open-source images.
en.explanation: Verified Publisher images come from commercial publishers verified by Docker; the badge does not say Docker maintains the images.

en.statement: On fresh Docker Engine 29 installs with standard settings, the containerd image store is the default.
en.explanation: Fresh Docker Engine 29 installations use the containerd image store by default; user namespace remapping is an exception.

source.title: containerd image store with Docker Engine

en.statement: `docker run -v cache:/data` fails when the named volume cache has yet to be created.
en.explanation: Docker creates a named volume during container creation if that volume name does not exist yet.

en.statement: When a container creates an anonymous volume, Docker names that volume after the container.
en.explanation: Docker gives an anonymous volume a random name that is unique on that Docker host. docker inspect shows it in the container's Mounts section.

en.statement: Removing a stopped container with `docker rm app` also deletes its named volume.
en.explanation: Removing a container leaves its named volume available. Removing the volume is a separate operation.

en.statement: `docker run --rm` removes an unshared anonymous volume when its container exits.
en.explanation: `--rm` cleans up an anonymous volume created for the container when it exits, unless another container still uses that volume.

en.statement: By default, `docker volume prune` removes unused named volumes.
en.explanation: Plain `docker volume prune` removes unused anonymous volumes. The `--all` option also includes unused named volumes.

en.statement: Docker copies existing container files into a newly mounted empty volume by default.
en.explanation: Docker initializes an empty volume from files already at the container destination. The `volume-nocopy` mount option suppresses that copy.

en.statement: Writes to a Docker volume pass through the container's writable image layer.
en.explanation: Volume writes bypass the container's writable image layer and go to the volume's underlying storage.

en.statement: On Linux, Docker's built-in `local` volume driver mounts NFS exports as volumes through its volume options.
en.explanation: The local driver passes mount options from volume-opt, for example type=nfs with addr and device, so an NFS share needs no third-party volume plugin.

en.statement: `--mount type=volume` uses key-value fields, while `-v` uses colon-separated fields.
en.explanation: For a volume mount, `--mount` takes comma-separated key-value fields; `-v` separates the volume name, container path, and options with colons.

en.statement: For a bind mount, `-v` creates a missing host source path as a directory.
en.explanation: For a bind mount, `-v` creates a missing source directory if the daemon has permission. `--mount` instead errors unless `bind-create-src` is set.

en.statement: A remote Docker daemon binds paths from the Docker CLI machine into containers.
en.explanation: A bind mount uses a path on the Docker daemon's host. A remote daemon cannot bind a path that exists solely on the CLI machine.

en.statement: A bind mount combines host files with existing files at its container destination.
en.explanation: A bind mount obscures files already present at its destination in the container. Docker does not merge the two directories.

en.statement: A read-only bind mount blocks host processes from changing its source files.
en.explanation: The `ro` option makes the bind mount read-only inside the container. It does not change access for processes on the host.

en.statement: On Linux, bind propagation defaults to `rshared`.
en.explanation: Docker uses `rprivate` for bind propagation by default. Submounts therefore do not propagate between replicas of the mount.

en.statement: With Docker Desktop, `rshared` propagates new submounts through bind mounts.
en.explanation: Bind propagation does not work with Docker Desktop, even when a propagation option such as `rshared` is specified.

en.statement: On a Linux SELinux host, `-v /src:/dst:z` labels the source for sharing across containers.
en.explanation: The `:z` bind option changes the host source's SELinux label so multiple containers can share it.

en.statement: On Linux, Docker removes files in a tmpfs mount when the container stops.
en.explanation: A tmpfs mount is removed when its container stops, so files written to that mount do not persist for the next run.

en.statement: On Linux, tmpfs files count against a container's configured memory limit.
en.explanation: Docker counts tmpfs usage toward the container's memory limit. Increasing the mount's size does not grant extra container memory.

en.statement: By default, `docker run` creates a new bridge network for the container it starts.
en.explanation: Without a network option, Docker Engine connects the container to the built-in default `bridge` network.

en.statement: On a user-defined bridge, Docker resolves container names through its embedded DNS server.
en.explanation: Containers on a user-defined bridge can resolve peers by name or alias using Docker's embedded DNS service.

en.statement: `-p 8080:80` maps host port 8080 to container port 80.
en.explanation: With `-p 8080:80`, traffic arriving at host port 8080 is forwarded to TCP port 80 in the container.

en.statement: With default daemon settings, `-p 8080:80` binds the host port to localhost.
en.explanation: With default settings, Docker publishes a port on all host addresses when `-p` omits a host IP.

en.statement: On Linux, `--network host` gives a container its own network IP address.
en.explanation: Host networking shares the host's network namespace, so Docker does not allocate a separate container IP address.

en.statement: On Linux, `--network none` leaves the container's loopback interface available.
en.explanation: The `none` network mode creates only the loopback device inside the container.

en.statement: `ipvlan` L2 mode assigns containers MAC addresses distinct from the parent interface.
en.explanation: In `ipvlan` L2 mode, containers use the parent interface's MAC address. The `macvlan` driver assigns a MAC address to each container interface.

en.statement: With `--network container:redis`, a container reaches Redis bound to 127.0.0.1 inside `redis`.
en.explanation: The container: mode joins the other container's network stack, loopback included, so a service bound to localhost in one container is reachable from the other.

en.statement: In Docker Engine 29, legacy links inject environment variables by default.
en.explanation: Docker Engine 29 disables legacy link environment variables by default. Legacy links are deprecated.

en.statement: The top-level `version` value selects the validation schema used by Compose v5.
en.explanation: The top-level `version` element is obsolete and informative. Compose validates against its most recent schema regardless of that value.

en.statement: Compose v5 uses a different Compose file format from Compose v2.
en.explanation: Compose v5 is functionally identical to Compose v2 for CLI and file interpretation; its main addition is an official Go SDK.

source.title: History and development of Docker Compose

en.statement: `COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME` takes precedence over the top-level `name` in a Compose file.
en.explanation: Compose takes the project name from the -p flag first, then COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME, then the top-level name, and then the base name of the project directory.

en.statement: By default, Compose connects services to a project network.
en.explanation: When services declare no network, Compose creates `<project-name>_default` and attaches those services to it.

en.statement: A Compose service uses a peer's published HOST_PORT for traffic on the default network.
en.explanation: Service-to-service traffic on a Compose network uses the peer's CONTAINER_PORT. HOST_PORT is for access from outside that network.

en.statement: `depends_on` waits for a dependency to pass its healthcheck by default.
en.explanation: Plain `depends_on` waits for a dependency to be running, not ready. The `service_healthy` condition waits for its healthcheck.

source.title: Control startup and shutdown order in Compose

en.statement: `depends_on` with `restart: true` restarts a dependent after a Compose restart of its dependency.
en.explanation: Nested `restart: true` propagates an explicit Compose restart or update of the dependency to the dependent service.

source.title: Control startup and shutdown order in Compose

en.statement: With profiles inactive, `docker compose up` starts profile-assigned services.
en.explanation: A profile-assigned service is excluded from a plain `docker compose up` when its profile is inactive, unless the service is explicitly targeted.

en.statement: `develop.watch` with `action: rebuild` keeps the existing service container running.
en.explanation: The `rebuild` watch action rebuilds the service image and recreates the service container with the updated image.

en.statement: When Compose merges `-f` files, it resolves relative paths from the first file.
en.explanation: Compose resolves relative paths in merged files from the base file, which is the first file supplied with `-f`.

en.statement: A user with rootful Docker daemon access can bind-mount the host's `/` into a container.
en.explanation: Control of a rootful Docker daemon permits creating a container with the host root filesystem bind-mounted into it, so daemon access belongs to trusted users.

en.statement: With userns-remap enabled in daemon.json, the Docker daemon runs as a non-root host user.
en.explanation: With `userns-remap`, container root maps to an unprivileged host UID, but the daemon still runs as root. Rootless mode runs both without root privileges.

en.statement: `docker run --cap-add=ALL` gives a container the same access to the host as `--privileged`.
en.explanation: Beyond granting all capabilities, --privileged opens access to all host devices and reconfigures AppArmor or SELinux; --cap-add=ALL only adds capabilities.

en.statement: The `docker-default` AppArmor profile protects `dockerd` by default.
en.explanation: Docker applies the `docker-default` AppArmor profile to containers, not to the Docker daemon.

en.statement: `docker run --user 1000` overrides the user named by the image's USER.
en.explanation: USER sets the default user for the image's first process, and the -u or --user option of docker run replaces it for that container.

en.statement: A secret supplied through `ARG` stays hidden from `docker history`.
en.explanation: Build arguments can be visible in `docker history`, so `ARG` is unsuitable for passing credentials or API tokens.

en.statement: `RUN --mount=type=secret` exposes a secret during one build instruction.
en.explanation: A BuildKit secret mount makes a secret temporarily available to the `RUN` instruction that uses it, rather than placing it in the final image.

en.statement: Docker Scout image analysis skips images lacking an SBOM attestation.
en.explanation: Docker Scout can extract an SBOM during image analysis and compare its packages with vulnerability data. An existing SBOM attestation is optional.

en.statement: Docker Hardened Images ship signed SBOMs and provenance with images.
en.explanation: Docker Hardened Images include signed SBOMs and SLSA build provenance so consumers can inspect image contents and origin.
